Incredibly, the placebo effect is (mostly) not real.

It is a result of statistical confusion. Whenever you have a group with extreme values, they tend to exhibit regression to the mean. Eg. on average, sick people tend to become more healthy over time.

Thus if you give one group medicine, and one group placebo, the placebo group will also tend to get better over time, because of regression to the mean.

People have then misinterpreted this to think that it is the placebo pill that actively does this. 

If you want to demonstrate a placebo effect, you have to construct a study where there are three groups: 
• A. treatment 
• B. placebo 
• C. no treatment, no placebo  

If B and C get different outcomes, that would demonstrate a placebo effect.

When this has been tried, mainly there has been no provable placebo effect. See the paper in the screenshot. (There is some evidence for an effect for pain, but this get's into a slightly different debate.)

The fact that the placebo effect is mainly not real, fortunately frees us from having to come up with convoluted explanations, as to why the placebo effect would work even when we tell the patient that it is a placebo, as in the quoted tweet.

1785737207984328942.text: PS this is mostly a public-facing summary of a lot of the key research in Science and Technology studies about quantification and data. I've got some of my own research that builds on this stuff, including:

1785737205937549338.text:
"The Limits of Data" is here. Tons more detail than this thread. Thanks to the folks at @ISSUESinST for encouraging me to write it!

https://t.co/Tp8kFkMFpA

1785737204326862962.text: My claim isn't that big data is false, or non-objective, or evil. It's to harness the power of big data, you have to systematically leave out a whole chunk of the world.

1785737202565329079.text: These qualities aren't accidents. They are precisely what enable large-scale data collection and aggregation, and create the power of big-data. But in order to do that, they have to systematically leave out a whole chunk of the world.

1785737200895996324.text:
To sum up: institutional data-sets tend to be

1. De-contextualized.
2. Collected using rigid categories, designed to somebody's interests.
3. And designed to be mechanically usable by anybody.

1785737199075594740.text: Mechanical procedures do get you a particular kind of objectivity. They make a certain individual bias impossible. But they also introduce another systematic bias - I bias towards what's easily and mechanically countable.

1785737197364392308.text: So if your data-collection procedure is supposed to scale, you want to target qualities that anybody can pick up. For example, the category of "good art" requires sensitivity to track. The category of "engagement hours" does not.

1785737195548184969.text:
Third thought, from Daston: institutions tend to want *mechanical procedures*. This means a procedure that can be executed by a replaceable worker. 

You don't want a procedure that requires particular sensitivity or experience. You want rules anybody can follow.

1785737193530798384.text:
Their example: in the ICD-10, the classification manual for disease which is the backbone of worldwide mortality statistics, there is super high granularity for urban accidents, but incredibly low granularity for rural accidents.

It represents the interests of urban people.

1785737191744024968.text:
For example, the US Census race categories emphasize the difference between "Asian" and "Latino", and forget the difference between "East Asian" and "South Asian".

These choices represent somebody's interests - but then we forget, and star thinking they're natural.

1785737189802061847.text:
Second thought from Bowker and Star: 

Every data-collection effort requires a stable classification system, in the background. Every classification system represents a choice about the data buckets. And every choice of buckets leaves out some info, and emphasizes other info.

1785737188094980456.text: So what enables the large-scale of data, and the easy agreeability of data, is that we've intentionally engineered out the high-context, highly nuanced bits. This is what enables data to travel between contexts.

1785737186249486496.text: To make data portable, we engineer a central nugget which doesn't need high shared context to understand. This is precisely what lets lots of people, from different backgrounds, collect and understand that data.

1785737184429158403.text:
First thought, from Porter, historian of quantification:

Data is powerful because it's "portable". This means it easily crosses contexts, and easily aggregates. 

But portability is a built, manufactured quality.

1785737182633996714.text:
Large-scale, institutionally collected data-sets will be biased away from the sensitive, the nuanced, the high-context. They will be biased towards collecting data on stable, easy-to-track qualities.

Data is systematically biased towards the easily countable.

1785737180813668841.text: So "The Limits of Data" is about the nature of large-scale data collection, and what gets systematically filtered out. This is not about racial or gender bias in certain data-sets (also a huge problem.) This is about the inherent bias of data, that arises from its core function.
